science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 6, 1572: A German astronomer discovers the Tycho supernova with the naked eye, but everyone thought the cosmic explosion was a 'new star'
science.description: null On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova with his bare eyes. He spotted the exploding star in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was as bright as Venus and could even be seen during the day. Astronomers were really confused, because it looked like a star just appeared out of nowhere. Schulër may have been the first to see it, but the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. Brahe studied it in detail and wrote a whole book about this so-called "new star." It then became known as "Tycho's Star." At the time, supernovas had not yet been discovered. Tycho's Star was finally classified as a supernova in the 1940s. Scientists now think it was a small star called a white dwarf that exploded thousands of years ago. Because Tycho's Star is 13,000 light-years from Earth, it took a while before anyone could see it. The Tycho supernova remnant as seen by the Chandra X-ray space telescope. (Image credit: X-ray: NASA/CXC/RIKEN & GSFC/T. Sato et al; Optical: DSS) Why it mattered The Tycho supernova, known technically as SN 1572 , is known today as a Type Ia supernova, which is a star explosion in a binary star system in which a white dwarf star draws material away from its partner, then explodes. But in 1572, the Tycho supernova appeared as something very different: a bright new star. While Schulër was first, other astronomers also observed the apparently new star in the sky. Tycho Brahe's numerous observations are the most well known, in no small part becuause he wrote a book all about them in "De Stella Nova" (Latin for "On The New Star." At the time, the prevailing theory among scientists was that the stars were unchanging, yet here was a new star -- a changed sky. "The 16th century exploding star, which appeared in the constellation Cassiopeia , was seen in daylight for about two weeks, and remained visible to the naked eye for 16 months," the University of California Berkeley wrote in 2004 . "Brahe's meticulous record of the brightening and dimming of the supernova now allows astronomers to identify its 'light signature" as that of a Type Ia supernova." "This was at the end of the Dark Ages in Europe, and these observations were an important piece of evidence that the heavens were not immutable," astronomer Alex Filippenko, who led a 2004 study on the origins of the Tycho supernova, said at the time . Today, astronomers are closely watching another star that might explode. Called T Corona Borealis , or the Blaze Star , the object is expected to be on the verge of exploding in a nova (a star explosion that is smaller than a supernova and may not destroy the star). is one of 11 known stars observed to have recurring nova explosions within gaps of 100 years or so. science.title: What's that bright 'star' in the early morning sky? It's not a star at all!
science.description: null Early morning risers heading to work or school before sunrise are likely to notice a very bright, star-like object appearing low in the east-southeast sky just before sunrise. What is somewhat amazing is that just a couple of weeks ago this object wasn't there at all, but now it literally stands out with such brilliance as to almost command the attention of commuters who might be traveling in an easterly direction to "Look at me!" The object in question is, of course, the planet Venus, which is currently amid one of its most spectacular forays into the morning sky, literally "vaulting up" into prominence. On Oct. 24, Venus came to inferior conjunction, passing between the Earth and sun and shifting from the evening into the morning sky. And the view is only going to get better in the days and weeks to come! Ascending in the morning In terms of morning visibility, Venus is now in a literal and figurative sense "rising to the occasion." It's now rising before the break of dawn, more than 90 minutes before sunrise. From here on, it will rise three minutes earlier each day, so that by Dec. 17 it will rise 3 hours and 50 minutes before sunrise and blaze in a completely dark sky for more than two hours before the first vestige of morning twilight. It will reach peak brilliance on Nov. 29, when it will shine at an eye-popping magnitude of -4.9. That's 12 times brighter than its nearest planetary competitor, Jupiter and a full 25 times more dazzling than Sirius, the brightest of all stars. If you live in a rural location with no light pollution to interfere, you might be able to make out that it is casting a visible shadow and if you follow it right on through sunrise, it will be evident to your naked eye in full daylight: a tiny white speck plainly evident against the blue daytime sky. In a way, we could even regard Venus as this year's version of a "Christmas Star," glowing with stunning radiance ". . . in the east" like the biblical quote mentioned in St. Matthew. What goes up, must come down After reaching its high point in terms of morning visibility in mid-December, Venus will start a long, slow slide back toward the sun, rising about 1½ minutes later each morning from New Year's Day through late March. By then, Venus will be coming up as dawn is breaking, roughly 100 minutes before sunrise. Venus will continue to get gradually lower and rise progressively later during the spring and by late June it will be coming up less than an hour before sunrise, ultimately vanishing into the bright dawn twilight by July. Venus will then go on a "summer sabbatical" of sorts and will not reappear again until about this time next year when it will begin a very fine evening apparition. So, if any of your friends or relatives remark to you that they saw a "strange UFO" on the way to work or school recently, you now can set them straight. It's not E.T. It's only Venus. science.description: Magnets can be made to levitate by the Meissner effect Science History Images / Alamy A tiny magnet that levitates within a superconductor trap may be the fastest spinning object visible to the naked eye, and one of the fastest spinning objects ever made. In the future, it could be used in experiments searching for mysterious dark matter particles and aid the development of quantum technologies. Superconductors are materials that conduct electricity with perfect efficiency, and they also expel any magnetic field that tries to permeate them – a phenomenon known as the Meissner effect. Because of this, a magnet placed above a superconductor experiences repulsive magnetic forces and starts to levitate. Tao Wang at the Agency for Science Technology and Research in Singapore and his colleagues have now set one such levitating magnet spinning at an unprecedently fast rate. Read more A miniature magnet rivals behemoths in strength for the first time The researchers used a spherical magnet made from neodymium, iron and boron that was about 30 micrometres wide, similar to the width of a fine human hair. They placed it in a cylindrical container made from lead, then enclosed that container in a chamber devoid of air, or a vacuum chamber. Advertisement Next, they used liquid helium to cool the whole setup to approximately -269°C (-452°F), only a few degrees above the coldest possible temperature . Under these extreme circumstances, lead behaved as a superconductor and the lack of air meant that the magnet could levitate within it without bumping into any particles. The team set the magnet spinning with a magnetic coil, ultimately pushing this tiny rotor to 138 million revolutions per minute. Wang says the magnet’s spinning was also very stable: it would take 17 days for its spinning speed to decrease by 50 per cent, something that would typically happen more quickly due to interactions between the magnet and its environment. “In terms of how many turns it makes before slowing down significantly, this is in the same league as the Earth’s spinning,” he says. “This, so far, is the fastest magnetically levitated rotor.” The record for the fastest rotating human-made object is also held by a levitated sphere, but that one was nano-sized, so invisible to the naked eye, and levitated by laser beams. Read more Physics of light and magnetism rewritten after almost two centuries Because the rotor experiences essentially no friction, and it is magnetic and cold, its behaviour is very sensitive to its environment, which makes it a promising sensor. The team has already successfully tested it as a gauge of vacuum at very low temperatures. Wang says this could be useful for builders of quantum computers, which often must be kept extremely cold and isolated in order to work. Benjamin Stickler at Ulm University in Germany says the levitated spinning magnet could also be used to precisely sense and measure magnetic fields. science.title: An unexpected feedback loop may be driving mega heatwaves
science.description: Land scorched by a fire in Wennington, London, during the record-breaking heatwave in 2022 Shutterstock Mid-latitude regions such as Europe are set to suffer more intense heatwaves than previously thought, according to new research that has uncovered a three-way feedback loop that amplifies extreme heat conditions. Heatwaves across the world have shocked scientists with their scale and severity in recent years, with heat extremes dramatically outstripping both historical records and the predictions of climate models. Read more Extreme heat is now making cities unlivable. How can we survive it? In the UK in 2022, temperatures exceeded 40°C (104 ° F) for the first time in history, despite predictions that such a milestone was probably still years away. Likewise, the 2021 heatwave in the Pacific Northwest saw temperatures hit extremes that far outstripped climate model projections. Advertisement Researchers have been scrambling to understand why very extreme heat is occurring more frequently, and with greater intensity, than expected at this level of warming. One team thinks the answer lies partly in the soil. Scientists already knew that high-pressure systems allow more solar radiation to reach Earth’s surface, heating up the land. They also knew that higher temperatures dry soils more quickly, removing the cooling effect provided by evaporation, thereby further amplifying heatwaves. Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter Now it seems that when temperatures climb high enough, dry soil, high pressure and extreme heat can amplify each other further, with dry soil helping to sustain high-pressure systems in the atmosphere. “Basically, the soils that are affected by circulation pattern also start to affect back on the circulation pattern itself,” says Kai Kornhuber at the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis in Austria. This three-way feedback effect makes extreme heatwaves 10 per cent hotter than they would otherwise be, according to the research by Kornhuber and his colleagues – a factor not fully accounted for in climate model projections. This will have serious consequences for our ability to cope with future extreme heat. “Ten per cent hotter or colder can really make a difference between a heatwave and a record-shattering heatwave,” says Kornhuber. “We’re facing so many critical thresholds in social and biophysical systems that an extra 10 per cent can really lead to temperatures that are then quite damaging.” Read more Is a broken jet stream causing extreme weather that lasts longer? This may include serious public health consequences, a breakdown of vital infrastructure such as transport links and energy grids, crop failures and the collapse of ecosystems. science.title: See the space race like you’ve never seen it before in PBS’s new living documentary, ‘We Chose to Go to the Moon’
science.description: null Straight from its inspiring live performance at New York City's Carnegie Hall this past April, RadicalMedia's filmed presentation of the immersive living space documentary, "We Chose to Go to the Moon," is finally available for the rest of us to watch. "We Chose to Go to the Moon" premieres Nov. 10 at 8:00 p.m. ET on PBS, PBS.org, and the PBS app, and we’ve got an exclusive clip to share featuring Mark and Kali Armstrong singing "Flight of Fancy." With a poignant introduction by Oscar winning director Ron Howard ("Apollo 13"), "We Chose to Go to the Moon" recalls the extraordinary saga of the global space race and Apollo moon landings by actors portraying pivotal persons who made it all happen. These roles include astronauts Neil Armstrong , Buzz Aldrin, Michael Collins and Ed White, Mission Control trailblazer Poppy Northcutt, " Hidden Figures " mathematician Katherine Johnson and members of the spacefaring families that remained on Earth, including Janet Armstrong and Betty Grissom. This dynamic multimedia production is directed by Tony Award winner Michael Mayer ("Chess"), combining a unique fusion of theater, concert and documentary storytelling using rare archival footage alongside historic flags and artifacts taken to the Moon and returned home. It also revisits the ill-fated Apollo 13 mission and adds a special tribute to moonwalker Neil Armstrong performed by his son Mark and granddaughter Kali. "We Chose to Go to the Moon" is created, written and narrated by historian John Monsky and stars Ian Weinberger ("Hamilton"), Skylar Astin ("Pitch Perfect"), Brent Comer ("The Outsiders"), Claybourne Elder ("Company"), Elizabeth Gillies (Netflix's "Dynasty"), Taylor Louderman ("Mean Girls") and Joy Woods ("Galileo"). Finally, Ian Weinberger ("Chess," "Hamilton") pulls it all together by conducting Broadway vocalists and the Orchestra of St. Luke’s in a selection of popular period music showcasing songs such as "Fly Me to the Moon," "Rocket Man," "Space Oddity" and "Sound of Silence." We hope space fans around the world tune in to experience this sensational stage show that honors America's human spaceflight history!

science.title: You can see another galaxy with the naked eye — here's how to find it
science.description: null The first time I showed someone the Andromeda galaxy (M31), our conversation did not go quite as planned. I'd carefully worked my way across the sky, starting from the Great Square of Pegasus and hopping from star to star until I was confident I had the right patch. I pointed the telescope, got M31 in its crosshairs and proudly announced to my wife that I had found the closest giant galaxy to the Milky Way . Would she like to see it? She then stayed quiet for a little too long as she looked through the eyepiece. Then came an unexpected question. "Is it near that little smudge?" Hmmm. "Err, no. It is that little smudge," I replied. There was a pause. Of course, I knew exactly what had happened. We'd both seen photographs of M31 — a vast spiral galaxy with a brilliant center, sweeping dust lanes and hundreds of billions of stars. What we were actually looking at was a grayish blur that could easily have been mistaken for a mark on the eyepiece. That apparent disappointment is now my favorite part of finding Andromeda because the unimpressive smudge is real. The light entering your eyes has been traveling across space for about 2.5 million years. No screen, photograph or telescope is necessary. You are intercepting ancient light in your backyard. Technically, the Triangulum Galaxy (M33), about 2.7 million light-years away, can be seen with the naked eye, so it is therefore the most distant object the naked eye can see. But not mine — I've never seen it. M31 is a much more realistic naked-eye target. What's happening and when to look The Andromeda galaxy is at its most dramatic in photographs, not an eyepiece. (Image credit: Created using Canva and a base image from Starry Night) Early November is an excellent time to find M31 from the Northern Hemisphere. It's high and well placed during the evening, and this week the moon is becoming particularly cooperative. New Moon falls around Nov. 9, giving us several evenings with little or no moonlight to wash out faint deep-sky objects. I usually begin with the star Alpheratz, one of the corner stars of the Great Square of Pegasus. You go two stars left, two stars up, and you arrive at M31. Another route — and a good way to check you're in the right place — starts in Cassiopeia, the distinctive W-shaped constellation high in the northeastern sky on autumn evenings. You can use its second V-shape as an arrow pointing straight at M31. You can do that star-hop with the naked eye or a pair of binoculars, but M31 is visible to the naked eye only under a very dark sky. However, don't look for a miniature version of the photographs. Expect a faint, elongated patch with a slightly brighter middle. There's another beginner trap to avoid. Images make Andromeda look compact, but its full apparent extent is enormous — several times the width of the full moon — and our eyes usually pick up only the much brighter central region.
